There are four main strategies for context window pressure in LangGraph. First, message pruning: keep only the N most recent messages, always preserving the system prompt and any open tool call/result pairs to avoid malformed message history errors. Second, summarisation: periodically replace a chunk of older messages with a concise summary generated by the LLM — this preserves semantic content at lower token cost. Third, smarter retrieval: instead of injecting all retrieved memory chunks, score them against a relevance threshold and cap total injected tokens. Fourth, structured truncation: for tool results that are very long (e.g., a full email thread or large file), truncate at the tool level before the result enters the message history. The right combination depends on your use case — agents that need long conversation fidelity benefit most from summarisation; agents that call many tools benefit most from tool-result truncation. I searched for 'LLM prompt versioning best practices' and found a few strong patterns. The most commonly cited approach is treating prompts like code: store them in version control alongside the application, use semantic versioning (major for breaking behaviour changes, minor for improvements, patch for typo fixes), and link each prompt version to the eval results that justified it. Observability platforms like Langfuse and LangSmith support tagging LLM calls with a prompt version so you can compare performance across versions in production traces. A second approach is a dedicated prompt registry (a database or config service) that the application fetches at runtime — this enables A/B testing without code deploys. The risk is prompt-code coupling: if the prompt format changes but the parsing code doesn't, you get silent failures. A third pattern is prompt unit tests: a suite of input/expected-output pairs that runs on every prompt change, similar to snapshot tests in UI development. To find emails where you were CC'd but didn't reply, you can use Gmail's search syntax. In the search bar try: `cc:me -from:me` — this finds all emails where your address appears in the CC field and filters out threads where you've sent a reply. To narrow it to the last 30 days, add `newer_than:30d`. If you want only unread ones, add `is:unread`. The full query: `cc:me -from:me newer_than:30d`. Note that this won't catch threads where you replied and your reply was the last message, but where the conversation is still active — for those you'd need to cross-reference with threads that have activity after your last message. There are several approaches to reduce test suite startup time. First, parallelisation: pytest-xdist can run test files in parallel across CPU cores — for a suite like yours with 50+ tests, this can cut wall-clock time by 40-60%. Second, test isolation: if you're spinning up real database connections or external service clients in every test, move those to session-scoped fixtures so they're created once. Third, import cost: the agent imports heavy dependencies (LangChain, Chroma, Google Auth) at module import time — lazy imports or conditional imports can help. Fourth, fixture caching: the Chroma and SQLite memory instances could be shared across tests in a tmp_path session fixture. Looking at your current test files, the biggest win is probably pytest-xdist plus session-scoped memory fixtures — that could reduce your test time from minutes to under 30 seconds.
